szoveg_eredeti:

Artificial intelligence can make celebrities and politicians appear to say things they never said. With the midterm elections approaching, experts warn that convincing deepfakes could make it harder for voters to separate fact from fiction.

Is that video real, or was it created using artificial intelligence? Not long ago, spotting a fake video or image was relatively easy. There might be something wrong with a person’s hands, unnatural facial movements, or a voice that didn’t quite sound right.

But AI technology has improved dramatically. Today, even convincing-looking videos of celebrities can be completely fabricated.

And with Election Day approaching, the consequences go beyond online scams.

A Fake Jaden Smith Video Shows How Convincing AI Has Become Researchers at Graphika, a company that investigates online threats and misinformation, discovered a series of social media accounts sharing a video of actor and rapper Jaden Smith.

In the video, Smith appears to be speaking Spanish and promoting giveaways involving major American banks, including Chase and Wells Fargo.

There’s just one problem. Smith never said any of it.

The video was created using artificial intelligence to make it appear that Smith was delivering the message.

“This is pretty decent quality video. The audio is pretty good,” said Tyler Williams, vice president of intelligence at Graphika.

Graphika identified nearly 30 accounts sharing the same video. Researchers believe the goal was to trick people into visiting a website and entering their online banking login information. Williams said Graphika’s native Spanish-speaking employees found the audio convincing.

What makes the scam particularly troubling is how little effort may have been required to create it. The people behind the video didn’t need Smith to participate. They could use existing footage of him available online.

What Happens When Deepfakes Target Political Candidates? The same technology used to impersonate a celebrity can also make a political candidate appear to say or do something that never happened.

That’s a particular concern with the November 3 midterm elections approaching. A fabricated video could show a candidate making an inflammatory statement, endorsing a position they don’t support, or behaving in a way that could influence voters.

But Williams says a fake doesn’t necessarily have to be convincing to spread.

People sometimes share AI-generated images and videos even when they suspect the content isn’t real, simply because they agree with the message.

“Yeah, I know that that’s fake. Like this image has 10 fingers on one hand, but like I feel like that. So I’m going to share that,” Williams said, describing how some social media users react to fabricated content.

That willingness to share something because it reinforces an existing opinion can help misinformation reach thousands or even millions of people.

Millions Being Spent on Political Ads Using AI Artificial intelligence is already playing a role in political advertising.

According to research by the Wesleyan Media Project reported by The New York Times, more than $137 million was spent airing political advertisements created at least partly with artificial intelligence. Researchers identified more than 220 such ads.

Not all AI-assisted political advertising is deceptive. The technology can also be used for ordinary production tasks. But some ads use fabricated images, voices, or video to portray political figures in ways that aren’t authentic.

‘One example involves an AI-generated depiction of New York political figures Kathy Hochul and Zohran Mamdani walking through the park. The video is much higher quality that AI-generated videos we’ve seen in the past.

The growing use of AI in political messaging raises questions about whether viewers can recognize manipulated material, particularly when watching videos quickly on social media.

How to Protect Yourself From AI Deepfakes Williams says the best defense isn’t necessarily learning to recognize every technical flaw in an AI-generated video.

He tells students in his intelligence courses to “interrogate your source of data.”

Before believing or sharing a shocking video, consider who posted it and why. Look for the original recording, check whether reputable news organizations have verified the claim, and be especially suspicious of videos designed to provoke an immediate emotional reaction.

A celebrity offering free money or a politician making an outrageous statement should be a reason to investigate, not immediately share.

And don’t assume that because a video looks and sounds authentic, it must be real.

There is currently no comprehensive federal law specifically regulating AI-generated political advertising.

However, 31 states have enacted laws addressing the use of AI or deepfakes in political messaging. Some require disclosures identifying AI-generated content, while others restrict certain deceptive uses of the technology.

For voters, the most important takeaway is simple: Before you believe what you see online, verify where it came from.

Artificial intelligence has made it easier than ever to manufacture a convincing video. That means seeing something with your own eyes is no longer proof that it actually happened.
